Hey! Thanks for the feedback and the questions.

> But now with explicit sharding this doesn't seem to work any more

I can't repro this. I ran this and it seems to work perfectly:

```
In [3]: jax.config.update('jax_num_cpu_devices', 8)

In [4]: mesh = jax.make_mesh((2,), ('x',))
WARNING:2026-01-29 09:55:36,816:jax._src.xla_bridge:876: An NVIDIA GPU may be present on this machine, but a CUDA-enabled jaxlib is not installed. Falling back to cpu.

In [5]: jax.set_mesh(mesh)
Out[5]: <jax._src.sharding_impls.set_mesh at 0x7f0530693220>

In [15]: def zeros_with_sharding(shape, sharding, dtype=None):
    ...:   return jax.numpy.zeros(shape, dtype=dtype, out_sharding=sharding)
    ...:

In [16]: @jax.jit
    ...: def some_fn():
    ...:     test_arr1 = zeros_with_sharding((32, 32), sharding_ax0)
    ...:     test_arr2 = zeros_with_sharding((32, 32), sharding_ax1)
    ...:     return test_arr1, test_arr2
    ...:

In [17]: sharding_ax0 = NamedSharding(mesh, P("x"))
    ...: sharding_ax1 = NamedSharding(mesh, P(None, "x"))

In [18]:

In [18]: test_arr1, test_arr2 = some_fn()

In [19]: test_arr1.sharding
Out[19]: NamedSharding(mesh=Mesh('x': 2, axis_types=(Explicit,)), spec=PartitionSpec('x', None), memory_kind=device)

In [20]: test_arr2.sharding
Out[20]: NamedSharding(mesh=Mesh('x': 2, axis_types=(Explicit,)), spec=PartitionSpec(None, 'x'), memory_kind=device)
```

> But there are still a lot of operations that are missing an out_sharding operator.

Please let us know which operations don't have it and I'll be happy to add it. Feel free to file issues with minimal repros!

> and therefore one can't use sharding.device_set or sharding.devices_indices_map to know which devices the array is distributed over

I claim that you have no reason to know about the devices ever inside jit. Just knowing about Abstract information is enough. In fact, that's how JAX tracing and lowering works. We only know about abstract mesh and that's enough for JAX to trace and lower to stableHLO.

And using `jax.typeof(arr).sharding` gives you enough information to know about the sharding to know how things are sharded. In explicit mode, you never really need to use `visualize_array_sharding`.

> Even worse without explicit sharding and outside of JIT jax.typeof(arr) seems to indicate that an array is unsharded, even if it isn't. The above code with use_explicit_sharding = False returns has sharding: False and a PartitionSpec(None, None)

This is documented in https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/notebooks/explicit-sharding.html#concrete-array-shardings-can-mention-auto-mesh-axis

Note that PartitionSpec DOES NOT give you the full information. PartitionSpec + mesh axis types has the full information. So P(None) + mesh.axis_types = (Auto,) does not mean replicated. It means that JAX does not know how this array is sharded and it's up to XLA to decide how to shard it.

Similarly if P(None) + mesh.axis_types = (Manual,), this means you are under shard_map and device-local view. If P(None) + mesh.axis_types = (Explicit,), this indeed means the array is replicated.

This is a mental model change in how sharding worked before explicit mode but the above explanation is the correct way to think about shardings on JAX type i.e. ShapedArray.

issue.body:
### Description

I have been writing a lot of distributed JAX code in the past and as Explicit Sharding seems to be getting more recommended I am trying to rewrite my code to use it everywhere.

While it seems like it makes quite a few things easier to reason about in theory and most of the code is pretty unaffected (the parts where sharding is not trivial already needed explicit handling), I feel like the way it is implemented now adds more confusion in some parts, even though things should be more explicit. 
This is especially noticeable in operations that create sharded arrays "from nothing" (things like jnp.zeros, etc. ; what the JAX docs call `nullary ops`).

I want to create a sharded array filled with zeros or other values.

In the past there wasn't really an elegant way to do this. But jitting the jnp.zeros with an `out_sharding` for sure was a guaranteed way to make sure the new array is sharded. (and in practice it worked out to never create unsharded intermediate data)

But now with explicit sharding this doesn't seem to work any more. Even with the very explicit `out_shardings=sharding`, the arrays are unsharded. With `use_explicit_sharding = False` this works as expected:

```python
import jax
from jax.sharding import NamedSharding, AxisType, PartitionSpec as P, Sharding

jax.config.update('jax_num_cpu_devices', 8)

use_explicit_sharding = True

num_gpus = jax.device_count()
sharding_type = AxisType.Explicit if use_explicit_sharding else AxisType.Auto
mesh = jax.make_mesh(axis_shapes=(num_gpus,), axis_names=('gpus',), axis_types=(sharding_type,))
jax.set_mesh(mesh)

sharding_ax0 = NamedSharding(mesh, P("gpus"))
sharding_ax1 = NamedSharding(mesh, P(None, "gpus"))


def is_sharded(sharding: NamedSharding):
    """
    is this data split on more than one device?
    """
    print(sharding)
    spec = sharding.spec
    for axis in spec:
        if axis is not None:
            return True
    return False


def array_info(arr: jax.Array, name: str):
    sharding: Sharding
    arr_type = jax.typeof(arr)
    sharding = arr_type.sharding
    print(f"{name}:\n{arr_type}\nsharding: {arr_type.sharding}")
    print("has sharding:", is_sharded(sharding))
    jax.debug.visualize_array_sharding(arr, use_color=False)


### Minimal example below

def full_with_sharding(shape: tuple[int, ...], fill_value, sharding: NamedSharding, dtype=None):
    # return jax.numpy.ones(shape, dtype=dtype, out_sharding=sharding) * fill_value
    def _full_with_sharding():
        return jax.numpy.full(shape, fill_value, dtype=dtype)

    func = jax.jit(_full_with_sharding, out_shardings=sharding)

    return func()


def zeros_with_sharding(shape: tuple[int, ...], sharding: NamedSharding, dtype=None):
    # return jax.numpy.zeros(shape, dtype=dtype, out_sharding=sharding)
    out = full_with_sharding(shape, 0, sharding, dtype)

    return out


@jax.jit
def some_fn():
    test_arr1 = zeros_with_sharding((32, 32), sharding_ax0)
    test_arr2 = zeros_with_sharding((32, 32), sharding_ax1)
    return test_arr1, test_arr2


test_arr1, test_arr2 = some_fn()

array_info(test_arr1, "test_arr1")
array_info(test_arr2, "test_arr2")
```
```
test_arr1:
~int32[32,32]
sharding: NamedSharding(mesh=AbstractMesh('gpus': 8, axis_types=(Explicit,), device_kind=cpu, num_cores=None), spec=PartitionSpec(None, None))
NamedSharding(mesh=AbstractMesh('gpus': 8, axis_types=(Explicit,), device_kind=cpu, num_cores=None), spec=PartitionSpec(None, None))
has sharding: False
┌───────────────────────┐
│                       │
│                       │
│                       │
│                       │
│  CPU 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7  │
│                       │
│                       │
│                       │
│                       │
└───────────────────────┘
```

Now of course the documentation would tell me to just use `jax.numpy.zeros(shape, dtype=dtype, out_sharding=sharding)` directly and indeed that works as expected. But there are still a lot of operations that are missing an `out_sharding` operator. For example `jax.numpy.full` has none. This again can be worked around (e.g. with `jnp.ones()*fill_value`), but this seems to go against the idea of making the sharding of jax.numpy operations explicit.

---------------

This is only slightly related (feel free to ignore it), but while creating the example above I noticed how hard it is to answer "is this array sharded?" (as in, is the data split across at least one axis.
In the past my logic was:
- outside of JIT one can just access `arr.sharding` directly and get a `Sharding` object (and nowadays a `NamedSharding` almost always)
- inside of JIT it is impossible to know the sharding at trace time, so for debugging `jax.debug.inspect_array_sharding` would return the right information after compilation or one can check the array shapes in HLO.

But with explicit sharding the documentation seems to be mostly looking at `jax.typeof(arr).sharding`. Which is nice that that works at tracing-time in JIT, but that comes at the cost of not being able to gain as much information as the Mesh is only an AbstractMesh (and therefore one can't use `sharding.device_set` or `sharding.devices_indices_map` to know which devices the array is distributed over).
Even worse without explicit sharding and outside of JIT `jax.typeof(arr)` seems to indicate that an array is unsharded, even if it isn't. The above code with `use_explicit_sharding = False` returns `has sharding: False` and a `PartitionSpec(None, None)`, even though the `jax.debug.visualize_array_sharding` shows the sharding.

### System info (python version, jaxlib version, accelerator, etc.)

```
jax:    0.9.0
jaxlib: 0.9.0
numpy:  2.4.1
python: 3.13.11 (main, Dec  8 2025, 11:43:54) [GCC 15.2.0]
device info: cpu-1, 1 local devices"
process_count: 1
platform: uname_result(system='Linux', node='standpc', release='6.17.13+deb14-amd64', version='#1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Debian 6.17.13-1 (2025-12-20)', machine='x86_64')
```
